final_answer: When an mRNA vaccine is injected, it enters the body and is taken up by cells, typically muscle cells at the injection site. The mRNA is encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles, which help it fuse with cell membranes. Once inside the cell, the mRNA is used as a template by the cell's machinery to produce viral proteins, such as the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2. These proteins are then displayed on the cell surface, flagging them as foreign. The immune system recognizes these proteins, activating B cells and T cells. B cells produce antibodies that target the spike protein, while T cells help destroy infected cells. The immune system also generates memory cells that "remember" the virus, enabling a faster response if exposed to the actual virus later. Importantly, the mRNA does not enter the cell nucleus and does not alter DNA. After the proteins are produced, the mRNA is degraded naturally, ensuring it does not persist in the body. This process primes the immune system without causing disease, offering protection against future infections.
